title: From Scorecards to Agents: A Survey of Anti-Fraud Models Across the Model-Risk Boundary, with a Focus on Evidence Traceability
content: The revised United States guidance on model risk management, issued in April 2026, applies its principles to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models, and places generative and agentic AI explicitly outside its scope. This survey follows the models used against fraud and financial crime across that line, from rules, scorecards, and statistical tests, through non-generative machine learning, to generative models and language-model agents, across six fraud types. Unlike prior surveys, we place all three generations in one decision-theoretic frame: we restate in one notation known results on cost-optimal and capacity-constrained alerting, undersampling calibration, and the identifiability of recall from alert feedback, express each generation's model, explanation, and validation quantity in that frame, and add two stylized models, one showing why mean aggregation dilutes the neighborhood signal of camouflaged fraudsters and one showing how verifier independence bounds the residual errors in a generated narrative. We find that statistical models and non-generative machine learning have mature validation practice anchored in supervisory guidance, that generative AI now appears both as a tool of fraudsters and as a component of defenses, and that in hybrid pipelines the generative component can write what an analyst or examiner reads although no dedicated supervisory framework covers it. We therefore formalize the evidence-traceability controls that can supply this missing validation as a division of verification labor, between the drafting agent, a deterministic field check, an independent verifier and the human examiner, governed by three parameters an institution can estimate; we then compare the generations quantity by quantity and close with a research agenda.
